nameStory: Harris's Checkerspot honors Edward Harris, a 19th-century naturalist and close friend of famous bird artist John James Audubon. Harris funded and joined Audubon on several expeditions, and this distinctive butterfly with its checkered wing pattern was named to commemorate his contributions to natural history. The "checkerspot" part of the name comes from the butterfly's wings, which look like they've been decorated with a checkerboard of orange, black, and white spots.
description: Harris's Checkerspot is a medium-sized butterfly with distinctively patterned wings that look like an intricate checkerboard of orange, black, and white markings. This member of the brush-footed butterfly family has a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2 inches across when fully spread. The wings show alternating rows of spots and bands, creating the "checkerspot" pattern that makes this species so recognizable. Like other brush-footed butterflies, they have reduced front legs that look more like little brushes than walking legs.

idTips.label: Checkerboard Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Wings display distinct rows of alternating orange, black, and white spots arranged in a checkerboard pattern, with the orange patches being particularly vibrant and eye-catching

idTips.label: White-Spotted Black Borders
idTips.description: Wing edges are bordered with black bands containing neat rows of small white spots, like tiny pearls sewn along the wing margins

idTips.label: Orange Wing Base
idTips.description: The areas closest to the body are predominantly warm orange with black veining, creating a glowing appearance when sunlight hits the wings

idTips.label: Reduced Front Legs
idTips.description: Front legs are much smaller than the others and held close to the body like tiny brushes - you'll see them using only four legs for walking

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a characteristic fluttery, somewhat erratic pattern close to the ground, often landing frequently on flowers or wet soil

habitat: Harris's Checkerspot thrives in wet meadows, bogs, marshes, and other damp areas where their host plants grow abundantly. Look for them in open, sunny wetlands from sea level up to about 1,700 feet elevation, particularly where flat-topped white aster and related plants are common. They're often found in areas that stay moist year-round, including the edges of ponds, streams, and in marshy fields throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, typically late May through early June, when you'll see them actively seeking mates and the first females laying eggs on host plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in early to mid-summer when adults are most abundant, feeding on nectar from various wildflowers and continuing to reproduce through July and early August.
seasonality.fall: Adults become scarce by late summer, with caterpillars feeding and growing on host plants through early fall before entering their overwintering stage.
seasonality.winter: No adults are visible - the species overwinters as partially grown caterpillars that huddle together in silk shelters near the base of host plants.

funFact: Harris's Checkerspot caterpillars are incredibly social creatures that build communal silk tents together, much like tent caterpillars, and actually huddle together through the winter in these cozy shared shelters - sometimes over 100 caterpillars will pile up together to survive the cold New England winters!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the Silvery Checkerspot, but Harris's Checkerspot has more distinct orange patches and cleaner white spots along the wing borders, while Silvery Checkerspot tends to be more muted with silvery patches on the underwing. Memory trick: Harris's has "hotter" orange colors - think "H" for Harris and "Hot" orange.
contextualKnowledge: This butterfly is considered a species of special concern in parts of New England and is believed to be extirpated (locally extinct) in Connecticut, making sightings particularly valuable for conservation efforts. Their dependence on specific wetland plants makes them vulnerable to habitat loss from development and wetland drainage.
compareHints: Harris's Checkerspot differs from its close relative, the Silvery Checkerspot, by having more vibrant orange coloring and cleaner, more distinct white spots arranged in neat rows along the wing edges. While Silvery Checkerspot shows silvery patches on the underwing surfaces, Harris's Checkerspot lacks these silvery markings and instead displays more consistent orange and black patterning throughout.
